nameStory: The Purplish Tagelus gets its name from the lovely purple-tinged coloration that often shows on its shell, especially around the edges and interior. The genus name Tagelus comes from a Greek word meaning 'a frying pan,' likely referring to the flattened, elongated shape of these clam shells that resembles old-fashioned cooking pans.
description: The Purplish Tagelus is a medium-sized clam that belongs to the short razor clam family, living buried in sandy and muddy bottoms of coastal waters. These clams have elongated, somewhat rectangular shells that can grow up to 4 inches long, with a distinctive gap at each end that never fully closes. Unlike true razor clams, they're more robust and less fragile, with shells that feel solid in your hands. They're filter feeders that extend siphons up through the sediment to draw in water for food and oxygen.

idTips.label: Shell shape and gaps
idTips.description: Elongated, rectangular shell with permanent gaps at both ends that never seal shut, unlike most clams - you can see daylight through the ends even when the clam tries to close

idTips.label: Purple coloration
idTips.description: Shell often shows purple or violet hues, especially on the interior and around the edges - the purple may be faint or quite vivid depending on the individual

idTips.label: Shell texture
idTips.description: Surface feels relatively smooth with fine growth lines, not as polished as a razor clam but not heavily ridged either - has a slightly chalky feel when dry

idTips.label: Size and proportions
idTips.description: Typically 2-4 inches long and about one-third as wide, giving it a distinctly rectangular rather than oval appearance when viewed from above

idTips.label: Siphon holes in sand
idTips.description: Look for paired holes in sandy flats at low tide - the holes are usually close together and may squirt water when you walk nearby

habitat: Found in sandy and muddy bottoms of protected coastal waters like bays, estuaries, and tidal flats throughout New England's coast. They prefer areas with good water circulation but not heavy wave action, often in the same areas where you'd find soft-shell clams. Look for them buried 6-12 inches deep in the sediment of intertidal and shallow subtidal zones.

seasonality.spring: Best time to find shells washed up on beaches after winter storms. Living clams become more active as water warms, making siphon holes more obvious in sandy flats.
seasonality.summer: Peak season for observing siphon activity during low tides. Shells found on beaches are often bleached white by sun, making purple coloration less obvious.
seasonality.fall: Good time for beachcombing as fall storms wash up fresh specimens. Clams are still active but beginning to burrow deeper as waters cool.
seasonality.winter: Clams burrow deeper and show little surface activity. Storm-tossed shells on beaches may show the best purple coloration, protected from summer bleaching.

funFact: These clams are like underwater vacuum cleaners - they can filter up to 5 gallons of seawater per day through their bodies, removing tiny particles of food while helping to keep coastal waters clean!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with soft-shell clams, but Purplish Tagelus shells have those distinctive permanent gaps at both ends and are more rectangular. Remember: 'Tagelus has permanent gaps, soft-shells can seal their flaps.'
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'short razor clam,' this species isn't closely related to the true razor clams that people commonly dig for food. The 'short razor clam' family name refers to their somewhat similar shape and burrowing lifestyle, but they're much sturdier and less fragile than true razor clams.
compareHints: The Purplish Tagelus is smaller and shows more purple coloration than its relative the Stout Tagelus, which grows larger and is typically more brownish or grayish. [UNCERTAIN: Limited reference material available for detailed comparison] The Purplish Tagelus also tends to prefer slightly sandier substrates compared to the Stout Tagelus's preference for muddier bottoms.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to its relative the Purplish Tagelus, the Stout Tagelus has a much thicker, more robust shell and lacks the purple-tinted interior that gives its cousin its name.
